Her voice came from the entrance of the shed. It was already distant, scattered, like a scrap of paper being carried off by the wind.
I didn’t look up at her. I looked at the damp cloth on the countertop.
"At the Shen hour, when the sun’s shadow reaches the crack at the base of the shed post, I’ll leave. You don’t need to wait for a sound—watch the shadow."
After saying this, I lifted the pen and continued making marks.
The next tag was passed over. I took it.
Hands were moving. The accounts were moving. The sun was slanting.
Before the Shen hour, those two crates had to be inspected. Aunt Zhao’s portion had to be delivered to the medical team. The accounts had to balance. The people had to stay steady.
**"Next."**
“Lin Zhao... if you don’t come at the shen hour, I’ll... I’ll take this notebook and sit at the committee’s door!”

I didn't lift my head. The pen finished making a stroke on the stub, then paused.
"Then you go."
There was no anger in that sentence, and no coaxing either. It was the truth.
"The booklet says 'shen hour,' signed 'Lin Zhao,' with a red line drawn. If you don't see me by shen hour, take the booklet and sit at the committee entrance—that's what you should do. It isn't making a fuss; it's filing a complaint. The words on the slip will speak for you. You don't need to shout yourself."
I turned to the next page of stubs and continued checking them off.
"But if you come running back before shen hour to say this to me again—the words written in the booklet won't change, and my legs won't grow faster just because you ask one more time. When what needs to be issued has been issued, and what needs to be inspected has been inspected, I will naturally go to the medical team. You just sit there and wait."
The pen stopped for a moment.
"You don't trust me; trust this booklet. The booklet is in your hands."
I looked up at her. She was still standing at the shed entrance, holding the ledger, leaning crookedly against the post.
"Go on. Sit and wait. Watch the shadows."
She didn't move. But she also didn't speak again.
Xiao Liu came over for the third time. This time he didn't support her—he just stood beside her and kept her company for a while. After a few breaths, Auntie Zhao turned on her own and walked east. Her steps were loose, but her direction did not waver.
I lowered my head, and the pen kept moving.
**"Next."**
The sun sank another inch. The shadow for shen hour was almost at the base of the shed post. Those two boxes still hadn't been inspected. Auntie Zhao's share still hadn't been delivered. The accounts still hadn't been balanced.
My hands could not stop.
"Lin Zhao... don't turn around later and say that notebook doesn't count..."

I set down the pen.
Not because of what she had just said—because everything that needed saying had already been said. To keep talking would be squeezing oil out one word at a time, and what came out would not be speech, but emptiness.
From under the counter I pulled out the stub book, turned to today’s page, and found Auntie Zhao’s line. Family member of C-47, one can of canned food, one ration, two water-purification tablets, one packet of broken rice flour, powdered ration pending issue at the shen hour. Three check marks beside it, with one blank still left.
I placed the stub book and the ledger side by side on the counter, opened to the same line, and let her see.
“This one on the left is the ledger. I wrote it. This one on the right is the stub. I wrote it too. The two match—the same handwriting, the same check marks, the same signature. When the committee audits the accounts, what they check is whether these two books match. If they do, it counts. If they don’t, then three years of accounts by me, Lin Zhao, are all wasted.”
I pointed with my finger at the same line of writing in both books.
“Look—are they the same or not?”
She lowered her head to look. Her lips stopped moving.
“Both books have your name written in them, both say what you received today. One is in your hands, one is here with me. If you tear up my copy, the one in your hands is still there. If you tear up the one in your hands—my copy is still here. You can calculate for yourself the odds of both being destroyed.”
I closed the stub book and pushed it inward on the counter—to a place she couldn’t reach.
“I’ll keep this one. The one in your hands, you take back to the medical team. At the shen hour I’ll come over, we’ll compare the two books, check off the final blank in person, and the goods will be handed to you. If you still think it doesn’t count—”
I looked up at her.
“—then give the book back to me right now. Once you give it back, then it really won’t count.”
She didn’t give it back. Her hands tightened, hugging it a little closer.
I picked up the pen.
**“Next.”**
